Appendix Appendix A Related Work A.1 Self-Evolving Language Agents Self-evolving language agents aim to continuously improve from their own interaction experience rather than remaining fixed after post-training ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2024 ) . One line of work primarily evolves the external agent system, including prompts, workflows, memory, tools, and other agentic structures ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Hao et al., 2026a ) . Automated agent-design methods search over workflow or program structures, while experience-driven agents continually refine explicit memories, reusable strategies, or dynamically constructed assets ( Yang et al., 2025b ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . These approaches demonstrate that accumulated interaction experience can improve future behavior, but much of the acquired capability remains mediated by an external scaffold rather than being persistently incorporated into the underlying policy ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . A complementary line of work directly adapts the agent model itself. Recent approaches use online parameter updates, reinforcement learning, self-generated tasks, reward models, or hindsight supervision to internalize interaction experience into persistent model capability, reducing dependence on external scaffolds and enabling subsequent behavior to improve as new experience accumulates ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026a ; Hao et al., 2026b ; Meng et al., 2026 ) . While these methods move self-evolution from the scaffold toward model weights, many rely on explicit verifiers, successful trajectories, or additional exploration to determine which experience should drive learning ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, we construct a data flywheel that does not use verifier-derived rewards for the core policy update, instead distilling privileged retrospective supervision from both the current trajectory and accumulated interactions directly into model weights, allowing the policy and its supervision to co-evolve across rounds. A.2 On-Policy Distillation and Privileged Context On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses the train–inference mismatch of conventional knowledge distillation by training the student on trajectories sampled from its own policy, while a teacher provides dense token-level supervision on those student-visited states ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . This formulation makes distillation naturally compatible with iterative policy improvement, since supervision is applied directly to the distribution induced by the evolving student. Recent work extends this idea by changing what information is available to the teacher. On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD) conditions the teacher on additional context while the student generates without it, allowing useful in-context knowledge, such as historical solution traces or optimized prompts, to be internalized into model parameters ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) further removes the need for a separate teacher model: the same underlying model acts as both teacher and student, with the teacher granted privileged information unavailable to the student; existing formulations commonly construct this privileged view from ground-truth solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Related self-distillation methods similarly exploit verified solutions, environment feedback, or successful rollouts as privileged signals ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Hao et al., 2026b ) . In contrast, our core method requires neither ground-truth trajectories nor verifier-derived rewards for model-parameter optimization. We construct privileged retrospective context from the agent’s own current trajectory and accumulated prior experience, and continually refresh this context as new on-policy experience is collected, coupling context evolution with model-weight evolution. Appendix B Implementation Details The prompt templates used for agent interaction, privileged-context construction, and frontier-guided context-policy evolution are provided in Appendix E . Training Configuration. We perform self-evolution for 10 rounds and sample 200 training instances in each round. Each round starts from the checkpoint produced by the previous round, while the accumulated experience bank is carried forward across rounds. We use full-parameter fine-tuning with forward-KL top- k k distillation, where k = 20 k=20 , a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} , one training epoch per round, and a mini-batch size of 48. No policy-gradient term or task-reward term is included in the OPSD objective. All experiments are run on a single node with eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Rollout Configuration. For ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA, the maximum numbers of interaction turns are 30, 15, and 15, respectively. The maximum prompt/response lengths are 4096 / 8192 4096/8192 tokens for ALFWorld, 2048 / 16384 2048/16384 for ScienceWorld, and 4096 / 4096 4096/4096 for SearchQA. Training rollout temperatures are 1.0 1.0 for ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA, respectively, with one rollout per training instance. The larger rollout group used by GRPO is restricted to the GRPO baseline and is not used by RSD . Teacher and Privileged-Context Configuration. The teacher retrospectively re-scores the student’s on-policy trajectories under privileged context and provides the next-token distributions used for distillation. By default, the privileged context consists of four components: precedents, accumulated lessons, turn-level reflection, and future hindsight over the current trajectory. To construct the precedent set, we first heuristically filter candidate trajectories for successful or useful experiences. For ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, success is determined by the environment completion signal, while for SearchQA we retain answers grounded in the top retrieved passages. We then rank the retained precedents by content-token overlap with the current task goal and retrieve the top two by default ( n n =2). For precedent ranking, we compute content-token overlap between the current task goal and each candidate trajectory. We lowercase and tokenize the text, remove punctuation and non-content tokens such as stopwords, and rank candidates by the number of remaining tokens shared with the task goal. Lessons accumulate reusable insights from previous experience, while reflection and future hindsight provide trajectory-specific retrospective information for the current turn. Following the stabilization motivation of prior OPSD work ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , we prevent the teacher from evolving indefinitely. The teacher initially tracks the evolving policy and is frozen at the best-so-far checkpoint once the benchmark selection metric decreases relative to its previous maximum; the frozen teacher is then used for all remaining rounds. This choice is motivated by a controlled teacher-schedule ablation in Appendix D.10 : a permanently frozen teacher remains stable but exhibits limited improvement, whereas a fully evolving self-teacher reaches substantially higher performance before collapsing in later rounds. Unless otherwise specified, all reported results use these configurations. Evaluation Protocol. For the main RSD evaluation, the evolved student is evaluated without privileged context, such that the harness is used only to construct training-time supervision. Privileged context is provided at inference time only in explicitly labeled diagnostic settings, including Harness@Inf, the internalization analysis, and frontier candidate probes. For ALFWorld, we evaluate approximately 140 valid-seen and 134 valid-unseen tasks and report success rate (SR) on both splits. For ScienceWorld, we evaluate 449 development variations and report task success rate. For SearchQA, we evaluate on the test set and report exact match (EM). Inference uses vLLM with fixed decoding settings within each benchmark. Frontier-Guided Context-Policy Evolution. The context policy is implemented as a YAML harness configuration and restricted to a predefined whitelist of context-policy and teacher-side re-scoring parameters, including precedent count and retrieval strategy, component activation, context position, and teacher temperature. The frontier model is not permitted to modify the underlying training algorithm or context-construction code. For frontier-guided context-policy evolution, we set the retrospective acceptance tolerance to ϵ = 0.5 % \epsilon=0.5\% , such that a proposed context policy is retained when its post-training environment performance is no more than 0.5 0.5 percentage points below the best previously accepted configuration. Baseline Implementations. We implement all comparison methods within the same training framework whenever possible and same training dataset size, changing only the optimization mode or supervision source. GRPO disables distillation and performs group-relative policy optimization with a rollout group size of 8 using environment success rewards. STaR iteratively fine-tunes the agent on its own successful trajectories. GT-SFT uses oracle successful trajectories for supervised fine-tuning, whereas GT-OPSD retains the same on-policy distillation objective as RSD but conditions the teacher on a gold successful trajectory instead of the experience-derived privileged context. For frontier-guided context-policy evolution, the Fixed Harness baseline keeps the canonical harness unchanged across rounds, while Random Harness samples edits from the same whitelisted YAML search space and under the same edit budget as the frontier-guided optimizer. The key internalization comparison is Evolved(no-C) versus Base(C): if the evolved model without privileged context outperforms the base model with privileged context, then useful information from privileged training has been transferred into the model itself rather than remaining dependent on inference-time context.
